A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same neuron-activation-based T2I backdoor defense, renamed from NaviDet to NaviT2I. The complete main texts, figures, tables, equations and appendices support comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original detection, timing, adaptive-attack and model-transfer experiments, plus dataset evaluations and ablations in the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds an activation-regularized adaptive-attack study and a BadActs comparison in Appendices E and F.

M1.justification: The detector's masking, activation scoring and thresholding remain unchanged. However, v2 introduces an attack-method adaptation for evaluation: Appendix E, Eq. (20), adds an activation-consistency regularizer to BadT2I training to suppress differences between benign and triggered inputs.

E1.justification: The MS-COCO and Flickr data, textual-trigger detection tasks, and backdoor target types are retained. The new regularized BadT2I experiment changes attack training within existing coverage; the BadActs comparison also uses existing attack tasks.

E2.justification: v2 adds BadActs, labeled BadAct in Table 10, as an evaluated comparator on RickBKD_TPA, BadT2I_Tok, VillanBKD_one and EvilEdit. The existing T2IShield_FTT, T2IShield_CDA and UFID comparisons remain unchanged. Other newly discussed defenses are explicitly excluded from evaluation.

E3.justification: Appendix E introduces a regularization-weight sweep from 250 to 10^-10 and evaluates image utility using FID alongside attack success, false triggering and detector AUC. Existing benchmark sampling, model versions, thresholds and timing procedures remain unchanged; cross-dataset threshold reuse was already documented in v1.

E4.justification: v2 adds a substantive robustness test that trains an attacker explicitly against the detector's activation signal, extending v1's trigger-form experiments. Appendix E examines whether evasion can coexist with successful backdoor injection and preserved image quality across regularization strengths. Existing ablations and trigger studies are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report mean and standard deviation for the 500-sample activation analysis and three timing runs. The new experiments introduce no repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or other changes to uncertainty-reporting practices.

E6.justification: Matched benchmark, timing and ablation values are unchanged. New Table 9 reports adaptive-attack outcomes, including detector AUCs of 93.6 and 95.7 at regularization weights 10^-9 and 10^-10. New Table 10 reports average AUCs of 60.7 for BadAct and 95.3 for NaviT2I over four attacks. These are additional comparisons, not improved scores for the unchanged detector.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.1, its Appendix B lemmas and proof, and the dual theorem and proof moved from Appendix F to H retain their mathematical substance. The removed standard attention exposition and the new experimental training loss do not introduce a revised theoretical argument.

C1.justification: v2 drops the abstract's claim to be the 'first general input-level' detection framework and presents an efficient defense framework. The central claims about early-step activation variation, broad detection effectiveness and low overhead remain. Explicit abstract references to UNet and DiT summarize coverage already present in v1.

C2.justification: Appendix E newly interprets activation regularization as producing model collapse or unreliable triggering at stronger weights, while weaker weights leave detection effective. Appendix F.2 attributes BadAct's failure on BadT2I_Tok to more concentrated malicious activation distributions. Existing explanations of trigger dominance, sentence triggers and style-trigger limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a promised code-release location and specifies the adaptive attack's regularizer and tested weights; the PDF does not establish that code is available. It also removes v1's explicit Q/K/V/O activation-selection description. Existing checkpoint references, hardware and timing details are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds eight cited works and a substantive comparison appendix. Appendix F explains the exclusion of unconditional-diffusion defenses, including Diff-Cleanse and TERD, and distinguishes the method from BadActs in methodology, theory and task applicability. This materially expands positioning against closely related defenses.

P1.justification: v2 renames the method, revises the title, abstract, introductory passages and author information, and expands the threat-model explanation. It shortens the preliminaries, moves the UNet block description to the ablations, and inserts new appendices before retained material. Most technical prose remains closely matched.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables 9 and 10, moves the pipeline illustration ahead of the prompt-switching illustration, and relocates several tables. Existing figures retain their visual content, and matched tables preserve their structure and values. Changes are additions and local rearrangements rather than a broad redesign.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's trigger-form tests, v2 directly tests an attack trained against the activation criterion and adds the relevant BadActs comparison. These additions strengthen robustness evidence and research positioning while retaining existing results. The gains remain limited by the narrow adaptive-attack study, sparse replication details for the new experiments, and removal of explicit attention-activation details.
